newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Crucial Zimbabwe budget may unlock foreign aid.
newsitem.headline: Crucial Zimbabwe budget may unlock foreign aid.

text.p: A budget that makes a serious attempt to cut Zimbabwe's chronic deficits sharply may make a crucial difference for the resumption of financial aid from Western donors.

The budget, unveiled on Thrusday, contained a surprise reduction in the budget deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) of 7.1 percent, much lower than a 10.3 percent forecast Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa gave Reuters earlier this month.

A 2.5 percent reduction in corporate tax to 35 percent and a 15 percent tax on pension fund profits and interest on treasury bills were the only other significant changes in Zimbabwe's largely as-you-were budget.
Murerwa gave no explanation for the improved outcome other than noting underspending of five percent and Z$922 million (U.S.$80 million) in profits from the central Reserve Bank.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank say they will study the budget and open talks with Zimbabwe in September on its bid for financial assistance, which was suspended two years ago due to missed economic targets.
The 1997/98 budget covers 18 months from July to enable Zimbabwe to align its financial year to the calendar year in 1999.

The World Bank and the IMF, which supported Zimbabwe's first five-year economic structural adjustment programme (ESAP), but withheld some aid before it ended in 1995 when the Mugabe government -- whose budget deficit has averaged 10 percent of GDP annually over the past 10 years -- missed some cost-saving targets.
The second phase of ESAP has been put on hold pending progress on the budget deficit and other issues such as reducing inflation and speeding up privatisation.
Murerwa promised to tackle all these issues quickly when he presented his budget and said the prospects of securing aid were bright.

"Economic prospects for the country look bright. Prospects for concluding negotiations on reforms are bright. This will trigger the resumption of much-needed balance of payment and budget support...," the minister said.

He forecast a budget deficit of over 8.9 percent in 1998. There will be a 28 percent increase in revenue, but spending will rise to Z$42.6 billion (37.7 percent of GDP), leaving an annualised budget defict of Z$10 billion.
Although Murerwa reduced corporate tax, when a five percent development levy announced last year comes into effect in January 1999, the tax will rise to 36.75 percent.
He also announced the introduction of a value-added tax in 1998, but gave no details on when it would take effect.
The only other significant tax change is a 15 percent tax on the profits of pension funds and making treasury bills subject to a withholding tax from January 1998.

Murerwa forecast a slowdown in the rate of GDP growth to 4.5 percent in the current year from eight percent in 1996, saying heavy rains would result in agriculture growing only 4.3 percent, compared with almost 50 percent in 1996. But manufacturing will grow more rapidly at six percent versus 1996's 3.5 percent.
He forecast average annual inflation of over 21 percent in 1997, but added that it would slow to 12 percent by the end of 1998 from 16.5 percent midyear.
